blockers: No dedicated profiler tool, profiling command, or documented performance-profiling/sampling workflow found for Quidra.
No documentation of IDE-integrated (visual) debugging (e.g., VS Code Debug Adapter Protocol support) beyond the terminal-oriented 'quidra debug' command.
metric.debugger_profiler_support.rationale: Quidra provides a real, documented debug workflow rather than just a bare entry point: 'quidra build --debug' produces an unoptimized, frame-pointer-preserving native build with dead-stripping disabled, and 'quidra debug FILE.qui' launches an actual native debugger (LLDB or GDB, or an overridable QUIDRA_DEBUGGER) against the resulting executable. Because code generation goes through LLVM/Clang, this gives access to standard native breakpoint/step/variable-inspection functionality via GDB/LLDB rather than a bespoke or undocumented mechanism. However, no dedicated profiler tool, profiling command, or documented performance-profiling workflow (e.g., perf/Instruments integration, sampling profiler, flamegraph tooling) was found in either the embedded specification docs or the project README. Separately, sanitizer-instrumented development builds propagate memory-safety instrumentation into generated native programs, which supports correctness debugging in CI but is not a profiler. This combination -- a real, standard-debugger-backed debug command but no profiler -- places Quidra in the middle tier rather than the top or bottom.
metric.debugger_profiler_support.rubric: 0-100 scale, frozen for symmetric application across all 10 languages. 0-20: no dedicated debugger/profiler command and no documented debug-symbol or stepping support. 21-40: a debug-oriented command or build mode exists but its interactive capabilities (breakpoints, stepping, variable inspection) are undocumented, and no dedicated profiler tool is documented. 41-60: a documented debugger with breakpoints/stepping/variable inspection (e.g., via DWARF + gdb/lldb integration) but no profiler tool. 61-80: full debugger integration plus a profiler tool or documented performance-profiling workflow. 81-100: mature debugger+profiler ecosystem with IDE integration comparable to mainstream languages.

source_evidence.quote: Sanitizer development builds propagate AddressSanitizer/UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer instrumentation to generated native programs as well as the compiler.
quidra build, quidra run, or quidra debug
quidra build --debug asks the native Clang driver for an unoptimized, frame-pointer-preserving debug build
quidra debug FILE.qui launches LLDB or GDB (or QUIDRA_DEBUGGER) against that executable.

blockers: No documentation of code completion, hover, go-to-definition, or rename/refactor support in the LSP.
No published editor-marketplace extension (VS Code, Open VSX, JetBrains, etc.) or adoption metric found for Quidra via targeted web search.
metric.ide_editor_support_quality.rationale: Quidra ships a first-party 'quidra lsp' server that is a thin client of the compiler frontend, reusing normal checking/diagnostics and the built-in formatter. The project's own documentation explicitly scopes this to an 'Initial' feature set (diagnostics, formatting, full-document sync over standard LSP stdio framing) with no documented completion, hover, go-to-definition, or rename/refactor support. Web verification found the same scope described in the project README and found no published VS Code Marketplace, Open VSX, or JetBrains plugin listing for Quidra (searches for a Quidra syntax-highlighting or language extension returned only unrelated languages with similar names, e.g. Quil and Quintry). This places Quidra in the low tier: real, compiler-integrated LSP/formatter tooling exists, but the documented feature surface is minimal and there is no evidence of packaged editor distribution.
metric.ide_editor_support_quality.rubric: 0-100 scale, frozen for symmetric application across all 10 languages. 0-20: no structured editor protocol (plain-text editing only, no LSP). 21-40: a documented/shipped LSP exists but is explicitly limited to diagnostics/formatting/document-sync (no completion, hover, go-to-definition, or refactor), and no confirmed published editor-marketplace extension (VS Code/JetBrains/etc.) is found. 41-60: LSP additionally provides completion, hover, and go-to-definition, and at least one published editor extension exists. 61-80: full-featured LSP (rename/refactor included) plus multiple editor integrations with meaningful adoption signals. 81-100: mature, widely adopted multi-editor support comparable to mainstream languages.

source_evidence.quote: The LSP server is a thin client of the ordinary compiler frontend
Initial LSP support uses the protocol-default UTF-16 positions, full-document synchronization, push diagnostics, and document formatting.
The built-in formatter reuses lexer token spans and applies only role-unambiguous whitespace edits.
quidra fmt FILE.qui --check is the non-writing canonical-form check used by automation.
quidra lsp provides compiler-backed diagnostics and formatting over standard LSP stdio framing
